metadata.title: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus Through Accumulation and a Water-Tank Model
metadata.description: A conceptual tutor module linking differentiation, integration, vertical offsets, initial conditions and steady-state behaviour.

core_idea.plain_language: Differentiation and integration are inverse operations in a qualified sense. Differentiating an accumulated integral recovers the original rate function, while integrating a derivative recovers the original function up to an additive constant.
core_idea.qualification: The additive constant appears because differentiation removes constant offsets.

part_1.statement: If F(x) = integral from a to x of f(t) dt, then F'(x) = f(x), assuming the usual continuity conditions.
part_1.intuition: F(x) records accumulated quantity. Its derivative asks how quickly that accumulation changes when x moves slightly, which returns the current value f(x).
part_1.summary: Differentiating an accumulation undoes the integral and reveals the rate being accumulated.

part_2.statement: If F'(x) = f(x), then integral f(x) dx = F(x) + C.
part_2.intuition: Integrating a derivative reconstructs the shape of the original function, but the derivative does not contain information about the function's absolute vertical position.
part_2.summary: Integrating the differential recovers the original function up to an additive constant.

vertical_offset_interpretation.two_dimensional_view: For an ordinary graph y = F(x), the constant C in F(x) + C shifts the graph vertically on the y-axis.
vertical_offset_interpretation.why: Every member of the family F(x) + C has the same derivative because the derivative of a constant is zero.

example.interpretation: x^2, x^2 + 5 and x^2 - 3 have identical slopes at every x and differ only by vertical offset.

variables.dV/dt: instantaneous rate of change of stored water

states.meaning: The tank is filling because inflow exceeds outflow.
The tank is emptying because outflow exceeds inflow.
The stored amount of water is not changing at that instant.

steady_state.definition: When dV/dt = 0 over time, the tank is in a steady state with respect to volume.
steady_state.balanced_flow: A key steady-state case is Q_in = Q_out. Water may still be flowing through the tank, but the stored volume remains constant.

boundary_cases.empty: An empty tank can have dV/dt = 0 if there is no net inflow. If water starts entering, dV/dt becomes positive.
boundary_cases.full: A full tank can have dV/dt = 0 if effective inflow and outflow balance, or if a boundary mechanism prevents stored volume increasing further. Fullness alone does not mathematically guarantee zero derivative.
boundary_cases.intermediate_level: At any intermediate level, dV/dt can also equal zero whenever effective inflow equals effective outflow.

water_tank_model.terminology_note: The mathematically useful term is steady state rather than solid state.

integral_as_accumulation.relationship: V(t) = V(0) + integral from 0 to t of [Q_in(s) - Q_out(s)] ds
integral_as_accumulation.interpretation: The integral adds all small net changes through time. V(0) is the initial condition and plays the role of the constant offset.

connection_between_rate_and_state.rate: The derivative describes local change: what the system is doing now.
connection_between_rate_and_state.accumulation: The integral describes accumulated history: how previous changes combine to produce the current state.
connection_between_rate_and_state.constant_of_integration: Knowing the rate history tells us how the state changes, but an initial condition is needed to determine the absolute state.
connection_between_rate_and_state.tank_interpretation: In the tank model, the constant of integration is the starting amount of water.
connection_between_rate_and_state.graph_interpretation: In a 2D graph, changing the constant shifts the function up or down without changing its derivative.

examples.name: Constant inflow, no outflow
examples.meaning: The tank gains five volume units per unit time. C is the starting volume.

examples.name: Equal inflow and outflow
examples.meaning: Water can continuously move through the tank while the stored amount remains constant.

examples.name: Changing net flow
examples.integrated_state: V(t) = V(0) + integral from 0 to t of r(s) ds
examples.meaning: Current volume equals starting volume plus the accumulated history of positive and negative net flows.

preferred_order: Explain rate of change versus accumulated quantity.
Introduce differentiation as extracting instantaneous rate.
Introduce integration as accumulating small changes.
Show why differentiating an accumulated integral returns the original rate.
Show why integrating a derivative produces F(x) + C.
Explain C as a vertical y-axis offset in two dimensions.
Use the water tank to connect rate, accumulation, initial condition and steady state.
Emphasise that dV/dt = 0 means no change in stored quantity, not necessarily no movement.
misconceptions_to_correct: Differentiation and integration are not unconditional exact inverses because integration introduces an arbitrary constant.
A zero derivative means the represented quantity is locally constant, not necessarily physically inactive.
Equal inflow and outflow can produce zero accumulation even while substantial flow continues.
An empty or full tank does not automatically imply a zero derivative.
